title: "2 · The replication: two's company"
---

::: milestone
**Block 3** · The same game, but played in groups of two to six. Does common ground still form when one person describes for a whole audience — and does the crowd change how fast it builds?
:::

## Needed, by whom?

Grice's speakers say as much as is *needed*. With one matcher, that's one person's common ground to track. Boyce, Hawkins, Goodman & Frank (2024) ran the exact game from Block 1 in **groups of two to six**: one describer, up to five matchers, everyone seeing the same twelve tangrams, six rounds. One description per trial has to work for the *whole audience* and each matcher only learns whether *they themselves* were right. 104 groups:

| column        | what it contains                                       |
|---------------|--------------------------------------------------------|
| `group`       | which group (`"group001"` ...)                         |
| `group_size`  | how many players: 2, 3, 4, 5, or 6                     |
| `trial` · `repetition` · `tangram` | as before                          |
| `message`     | one describer message                                  |
| `n_words`     | its length                                             |
| `n_correct`   | how many matchers picked right on this trial           |
| `n_matchers`  | how many matchers there were (`group_size - 1`)        |

<a class="btn btn-primary" href="multiparty_teaching.csv" download>
⬇ multiparty_teaching.csv</a>

``` r
multiparty <- read.csv("multiparty_teaching.csv")
glimpse(multiparty)
```

## Task 1: The measure has to match the unit

In this dataset, the describer often sends several short messages for one shape rather than one long one, so we want the total words spent on each shape each round. That means two steps: sum the words within each trial, then average those totals per group size and round.

``` r
# Step 1: total describer words in each trial.
per_trial <- multiparty %>%
  group_by(group, group_size, repetition, trial) %>%
  summarise(words = sum(n_words), .groups = "drop")

# Step 2: average those totals, per group size and round.
red_multi <- per_trial %>%
  group_by(group_size, repetition) %>%
  summarise(mean_words = mean(words), .groups = "drop")

red_multi
```

``` repl
# A tibble: 30 × 3  (your table: here as size x repetition)
repetition      2     3     4     5     6
1            21.7  23.2  27.3  27.3  24.9
2            15.8  15.9  18.2  25.9  17.5
3            10.7  13.0  14.1  15.4  18.1
4             8.2   8.8  11.5  13.3  13.4
5             5.7   6.1   9.1  10.2  11.3
6             5.2   6.0   6.6   6.8   7.3
```

## Task 2: Five curves on one plot

Putting `colour =` inside `aes()` draws a separate line for each value of a variable. Here, one line per group size. We wrap it in `factor()` so R treats the sizes as five distinct categories to colour, not as numbers on a scale:

``` r
ggplot(red_multi, aes(x = repetition, y = mean_words,
                      colour = factor(group_size))) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  labs(title = "Everyone gets shorter, but big groups take a little longer",
       x = "repetition", y = "mean words per description",
       colour = "group size") +
  theme_bw()
```

:::: {.predict-check data-answer="slower" data-accept="slower||big groups slower||they take longer||more slowly||the big groups are slower||crowds are slower"}
Every line falls to about the same place by round six. Do all the groups get there at the same *speed*, or do some shrink faster than others?

::: {.pc-explanation}
The bigger the group, the slower the shrink. Everyone lands near the floor by round six. Pairs around 5 words, six-player groups around 7, but they get there very differently: at round three, pairs are already down to about 11 words while six-player groups are still near 18. Common ground with five people is slower to form than with one.
:::
::::

## Task 3: What does the crowd cost in accuracy?

Now the other half: did the bigger groups understand as well? One care-step first. `n_correct` is recorded on every message in a trial, so the same trial's score appears several times. We want each trial counted once. `distinct()` keeps one row per trial:

``` r
multiparty %>%
  distinct(group, trial, .keep_all = TRUE) %>%   # one row per trial, not per message
  group_by(group_size, repetition) %>%
  summarise(pct_correct = 100 * mean(n_correct / n_matchers)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = repetition, y = pct_correct,
             colour = factor(group_size))) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  labs(title = "Pairs reach near-perfect. Big groups never quite do",
       x = "repetition", y = "% of matchers correct",
       colour = "group size") +
  theme_bw()
```

``` repl
% matchers correct, size x repetition:
repetition      2     3     4     5     6
1            82    83    84    78    80
2            89    87    88    84    85
6            97    91    87    83    86
```

Pairs finish near 97% correct. Six-player groups level off in the mid-80s, and they got there using slightly *more* words. More said, less understood, per listener: the mirror image of what pairs achieved.


## Discuss with your neighbour

Why would five matchers make common ground harder to build?

::: milestone
**Where this leaves the theory.** The core finding held at every group size: describe something repeatedly and the description shrinks. That's a robust phenomenon. But *how fast* it shrinks depends on the audience. Common ground is built through back-and-forth, and that back-and-forth gets thinner when it's split five ways.
:::
